title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 428
paragraphs: This, they say, was the first beginning of Cambyses's evil deeds; and next, after this, he put to death his sister, who had accompanied him to Egypt and to whom he was also married, she being his sister by both parents. He had taken her in marriage in the following manner (for before this the Persians had not been accustomed at all to marry their sisters). Cambyses fell in love with one of his sisters and wished to take her to wife; so, since he had it in mind to do what was not customary, he called the Royal Judges and asked them whether there was any law permitting one who desired to marry his sister. Now the Royal Judges are men chosen from among the Persians, and they hold office until they die or until some injustice is found in them — that long, and no longer. They pronounce decisions for the Persians and are the expounders of the ancestral ordinances, and all matters are referred to them. When Cambyses asked them, they gave him an answer that was both upright and safe, saying that they had found no law permitting a brother to marry his sister, but apart from that they had found a law to the effect that the king of the Persians might do whatever he wished. Thus on one hand they did not tamper with the law out of fear of Cambyses, while at the same time, to avoid perishing themselves by upholding the law, they found another law alongside the one asked about, in favor of the man who wanted to marry his sisters. So Cambyses at that time took as his wife the one he was in love with, but not long afterwards he took another sister as well. Of these, it was the younger whom he put to death, she having accompanied him to Egypt.
